---
title: "Preprocessing: study band and mains removal"
---

## Objective

Restrict a record to a **study band** $[f_{min}, f_{max}]$ (default: low-pass 100 Hz) and
optionally remove the **mains line** (50 Hz, configurable) and its harmonics, before noise
and sine analyses. The band-limited data and its **noise-equivalent bandwidth (ENBW)** are
returned, so that every RMS value can be traced to the bandwidth it was measured in.

## Principle and equations

**Detrending** removes the mean (`constant`, default) or a least-squares line (`linear`).

**FFT mask (default, `filter_method="fft"`).** With $X_k$ the real FFT of the $N$ samples
($f_k = k f_s / N$), the filtered record is

$$
y_n = \mathrm{IFFT}\left(X_k \cdot \mathbb{1}\left[f_{min} \le f_k \le f_{max}\right]
\cdot \prod_{m} \mathbb{1}\left[|f_k - m f_{mains}| > w/2\right]\right),
$$

where $w$ is `mains_width` (default 1 Hz, i.e. ±0.5 Hz). By Parseval's theorem the variance of
$y$ is the power of the kept bins, and the ENBW is the width of the kept bins:

$$
\mathrm{ENBW} = \frac{f_s}{N}\sum_{k\ \mathrm{kept}} c_k, \qquad c_k = \tfrac12 \text{ at DC and Nyquist, } 1 \text{ elsewhere}.
$$

**Butterworth (`filter_method="iir"`).** A Butterworth filter of order `filter_order` is
applied forward and backward (`scipy.signal.sosfiltfilt`), with `iirnotch` filters of quality
factor $Q = f/w$ at the mains lines. The forward-backward filter has the power response
$|H(f)|^4$, hence

$$
\mathrm{ENBW} = \int_0^{f_s/2} |H(f)|^4 \, df .
$$

For an analog order-4 Butterworth this gives $\mathrm{ENBW} \approx 0.898\,f_c$: the white-noise
RMS is about 5 % below the value of the nominal band. The software always computes and reports
the actual ENBW (numerically, from `sosfreqz`).

**Mains lines** are $k \cdot f_{mains}$ for $k = 1 \dots K$ with $k\,f_{mains} \le f_{max}$
(all lines by default, or `mains_harmonics`).

## Assumptions and validity

- The FFT mask treats the record as periodic: the jump between the last and first samples
  spreads a little energy over all frequencies. It is negligible for long noise records; use
  `detrend="linear"` when the record drifts.
- When `fmax` is at or above Nyquist no low-pass is applied: the band is limited by the
  sampling and a warning says so.
- With the IIR method, filter transients are removed at both ends: the impulse response is
  computed and the samples holding 99.9 % of its energy are trimmed (at most 10 % of the
  record).

## Numerical implementation

`processing.band.band_limit` uses `scipy.fft.rfft`/`irfft` (multi-threaded) for the mask, and
`scipy.signal.butter`, `iirnotch`, `tf2sos`, `sosfiltfilt` and `sosfreqz` (65 536 points) for
the IIR method. The FFT mask is the default because its bandwidth is exact, its phase is zero
and it is consistent with the integration of the PSD (see [Spectra](spectra.qmd)).

## Limits, biases and uncertainty

- Removing the mains lines also removes the noise inside the excluded zones: the ENBW is
  reduced accordingly (98.5 Hz for a 0–100 Hz band with 50 and 100 Hz removed). The RMS is
  therefore the RMS *in the reported ENBW*.
- A brick-wall mask rings in the time domain: peak-to-peak values of filtered noise are
  slightly larger than with a smooth filter.
- The IIR ENBW departs from the analog value near Nyquist (bilinear transform warping).

## Validation

| Case | Expected | Test |
|---|---|---|
| White noise, σ = 100 counts, band 0–50 Hz at 200 Hz | RMS = 100/√2, ENBW = 50 Hz | `test_band_limited_white_noise` |
| 50 Hz line of 50 counts + unit noise, mains removed | RMS = √(98.5/500), ENBW 98.5 Hz | `test_mains_removal_and_enbw` |
| IIR order 4, $f_c$ = 5 Hz at 200 Hz | ENBW = 0.898 $f_c$ ± 1 %; RMS follows the ENBW | `test_iir_band_reports_effective_enbw` |

## Worked example

```{python}
import numpy as np
from onthesignal.processing import band_limit

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fs, n = 1000.0, 400_000
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n) + 50 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50 * np.arange(n) / fs)
for method in ("fft", "iir"):
    out = band_limit(x, fs, fmax=100, remove_mains=True, method=method)
    print(f"{method}: RMS = {out.data.std():.4f}, ENBW = {out.enbw:.2f} Hz, "
          f"removed lines = {out.removed_lines}")
```
